frames.narration: At 08:20 an order is placed. The order service creates a timer: in 40 minutes, at 09:00:00, call back to cancel the order if it is still unpaid. The API gives it the id t-501.

The timer is stored under the bucket 09:00:00, which covers the 10 seconds from 09:00:00 to 09:00:10, and under the exact time and id. It is stored on three copies before the API says yes, and an index maps t-501 to this bucket for cancels.

At 08:55 the node that owns t-501's partition reads the bucket 09:00:00, five minutes ahead, about 52,000 timers. Five minutes is 30,000 ticks of 10 ms, more than the 4,096 the middle wheel covers, so t-501 goes into the coarsest of the three wheels.

As time passes, t-501 moves down. About 40 seconds before 09:00:00 it moves into the middle wheel, and less than a second before it moves into the finest wheel, in the slot for its exact tick. Nobody scans the other 52,000 timers to find it.

The tick 09:00:00.000 comes. The node claims t-501 in the store with a lease of 30 seconds. The claim is a conditional write, and it succeeds only if t-501 still exists and nobody else holds it, so a cancel or a second node would have stopped it here.
The node puts the message on the delivery queue with the key t-501 and the attempt number 1, and the queue hands it to the order service. It is sent 4 ms after the fire time, never before it.

The order service looks up t-501 in its dedup table. It has not seen it, so it records it and acts: the order is unpaid, so it is cancelled. Had the node crashed after sending, the lease would expire at 09:00:30, another node would send attempt 2, and the dedup table would drop it.
The order service acknowledges. Only now does the node delete the timer, so the store holds one fewer timer and the lateness metric gets a 4 ms point for the 99th-percentile graph.
